The family has undergone a significant shift from a self-sustaining unit to a compact group of minimal size. In Western advanced societies, the large consanguine family has been replaced by the smaller, independent nuclear family. The prevalence of joint families is diminishing in India, with independent families on the rise, particularly in urban areas. The functions of the family have changed due to modern industrialism and urbanism, affecting both its structure and functions.
Traditionally, the family satisfied sexual needs primarily within marriage, but there is now growing acceptance of pre-marital and extra-marital sexual relations in Western societies.
In Western societies, some couples choose not to have children, and women sometimes become mothers without marriage, reflecting a shift in reproduction practices.

The role of the family in providing sustenance has been taken over by hospitals and nursing homes, which offer superior medical care. Government and non-government organizations also provide protection and care for the elderly.
With the rise of industrial work, women have less time for socializing with children, reducing the family's role as a primary agent of socialization.
The traditional agricultural family has lost significance as a self-sufficient economic unit, transitioning to a consumer unit with many functions outsourced to external entities.
The family has largely outsourced its educational responsibilities to nursery schools, kindergartens, and technical institutions, significantly diminishing its role in education.
The family's role in religious training has gradually diminished, with less engagement in religious activities compared to the past.
The family no longer plays a central role in providing recreation; contemporary recreation is largely sought outside the home at clubs and other venues.

The family has seen a significant transformation, outsourcing many of its previous responsibilities such as education, religion, recreation, and protection to external entities, leading to a reduction in its functions.

Despite functional changes, the family retains a distinctive position among institutions, characterized as 'a unity of interacting personalities'. The modern family is more individualized and democratic, with elevated prestige and position for women.
Leslie Bosch, PhD
